title: A Buyer’s Guide to Choosing the Right Retail Operations Software (2026)
summary: A practical guide to retail operations software: what it is and how to choose tools that connect store operations.
body_markdown:
Retail operations software helps store owners keep operations efficient and connected. Without it, the customer experience might be disconnected, and your retail team might lose time reconciling separate databases and platforms.


According to new[Coresight research](https://9302266.fs1.hubspotusercontent-na1.net/hubfs/9302266/Innovator%20Report/Simbe-The%20State%20of%20In-Store%20Retailing%202026%202.pdf?__hstc=6278124.6d268efe08bdcdd752e48a0979179fd7.1782102144808.1782102144808.1782102144808.1&__hssc=6278124.1.1782102144808&__hsfp=b18b72698c0991b53f99a886a946c83f) , a lack of software integration costs businesses $196.4 billion in inefficiencies. Not to mention[nearly 89% of retailers](https://your.servicenow.com/2026retailreport/items/retail-report---2026) are still somewhat reliant on manual processes to run their stores day to day.


With retail operations software in place, business owners can establish a single source of truth for store data, manage in-store and online orders from the same platform, and personalize the[customer journey](https://www.shopify.com/blog/how-to-map-out-the-customer-journey-for-your-retail-business) for a better shopping experience. Ahead, learn how to choose one, and whether a[unified commerce platform like Shopify](https://www.shopify.com/blog/unified-commerce) is right for you.

## What is retail operations software?


Retail operations software helps you manage the systems and workflows behind day-to-day[store operations](https://www.shopify.com/blog/retail-operations) . That includes:


- Inventory
- Orders
- Pricing
- Returns
- Fulfillment
- Staff tasks
- Customer information
- Reporting
- Communication between stores and headquarters


### Retail operations software vs. POS, WMS, and ERP


Retail operations software isn’t the same as a[point-of-sale (POS) system](https://www.shopify.com/blog/point-of-sale-system) , warehouse management system (WMS), or enterprise resource planning (ERP), but it often connects with all of them:


- A POS system helps stores process sales and manage checkout, and some POS systems also include inventory, customer, and order data.
- A WMS manages inventory movement in warehouses and distribution centers.
- An ERP manages broader business functions like finance, procurement, and supply chain, but it may not give store teams a shelf-level view.


For retailers already selling online with Shopify,[Shopify POS](https://www.shopify.com/pos) can extend the same back office into physical retail. The platform connects in-person selling with online sales, inventory, staff permissions, reporting, and more, so store teams and ecommerce teams can work from the same commerce system.


## Why do you need retail operations software in 2026?


Inefficient retail operations not only cost businesses money, they also create a negative[customer experience](https://www.shopify.com/blog/customer-experience-strategy) .[ServiceNow’s 2026 survey](https://your.servicenow.com/2026retailreport/items/retail-report---2026) showed that inconsistent store data leads to excessive wait times at checkout (38% of retailers), inventory errors (38%), increased associate workload (37%), and less time for staff to engage with customers (32%).


By unifying customer data and providing integrated support for retail associates, retail operations software creates a more efficient experience for your customers and staff. When[Elite Eleven](https://eliteelevensporting.com/) , an Australian sportswear brand, opened their first retail store, they used the same POS system they’d used for their pop-up stores. The only problem was that it didn’t integrate with the brand’s online Shopify store, or their third-party inventory management system, which ended up creating data silos.


“Previously, we had no ability to get a single view of inventory in store and online,” founder and CEO Benn Martiniello says. “This fragmentation meant we weren’t able to stock stores very well."


After adopting Shopify POS to unify their in-store and online data,[Elite Eleven saw 240% year-over-year retail sales growth](https://www.shopify.com/case-studies/elite-eleven) and began processing more than 30 ship-to-customer orders daily.


“Moving to the Shopify platform was a no-brainer—we now have one unified commerce system across online and offline stores to understand our customers and serve the most relevant products,” says Benn.


## The key features to look for in retail operations software


Like[unified commerce](https://www.shopify.com/blog/unified-commerce) platforms, retail operations software unifies store data across channels. There are five features to keep in mind when choosing the software that best fits your business:


### Unified inventory visibility


A unified inventory gives you visibility into a sale on the floor, an online order, and a backroom count. Real-time data exchange is at the top of[Gartner’s guide](https://www.gartner.com/en/documents/6994666) to choosing a unified commerce platform, as it impacts the accuracy of all the other features.


Shopify store owners, for example, get access to inventory that syncs across locations and channels. Store teams can send, receive, and update inventory quantities directly in Shopify POS, while[permission controls](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/your-account/users/roles/permissions) limit who can make critical changes. Shopify also tracks inventory actions with an audit trail, so you can see where changes came from.


[Venus et Fleur](https://www.venusetfleur.com/) ’s Eternity flowers sell in high volume around holidays, and tracking stock across both ecommerce and retail locations grew complicated during these seasonal demand surges. After the brand[unified their channels on Shopify](https://www.shopify.com/case-studies/venus-et-fleur) , real-time inventory data gave store associates what they needed to cross-sell and upsell in person.


“Shopify has streamlined our operations by enabling us to manage all of our sales channels in one place,” says Brendan Gorman, head of ecommerce.


### Online sales and store continuity


A busy store shouldn’t have to suspend sales because the Wi-Fi drops or because the building has patchy mobile coverage.


Shopify POS supports offline checkout and[offline card payments](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/sell-in-person/shopify-pos/selling-offline/offline-payments) for eligible setups. When the device reconnects, Shopify processes saved card payments, syncs orders with Shopify admin, and connects customer information to the right order.


When[NEOM Wellbeing](https://neomwellbeing.com/) switched to Shopify, they knew they didn’t have to worry about their Wellbeing Hubs with limited mobile and Wi-Fi connectivity. After[implementing Shopify POS](https://www.shopify.com/case-studies/neom-wellbeing) , retail teams knew they could continue taking payments offline and supporting customers—part of a Shopify POS rollout that helped lift checkout conversion 34% and order volume 10%.


“We’ve tripled in size since we first started on Shopify, and the platform has grown with us,” says Clare Jerome, NEOM’s technology product manager.

### Advanced reporting and analytics


With advanced reporting and analytics, dashboards and reporting modules turn operational data into actionable decisions.


Shopify’s analytics give you a[customizable dashboard](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/reports-and-analytics/shopify-reports/overview-dashboard/customizing-overview-dashboard) that surfaces metrics like net sales by channel or sessions by device type, and each card opens into a deeper report for further exploration. Live View shows store traffic as it happens, while Reports compile data into graph and table form, organized by category so you can filter to the question you’re asking.


When the defaults don’t cover it, you can[build custom reports](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/reports-and-analytics/shopify-reports/report-types/custom-reports/create-custom-explorations) using ShopifyQL.


[Good Ranchers](https://www.goodranchers.com/) , for example, used Shopify Analytics to fix a retention problem they could see but not explain. When they dug into their Shopify analytics, the team found that customer drop-off spiked after the second order.


To address the trend, they[added a free mystery gift to every third order](https://www.shopify.com/case-studies/good-ranchers) . It worked, and in conjunction with their broader Shopify migration they saw 48% year-over-year revenue growth and a 10% lift in subscription adoption.


### Open architecture and integrations


Your operations layer has to connect to everything else you run without forcing you to rebuild data flows every time something changes.


Shopify supports that kind of setup through application programming interfaces (APIs),[webhooks](https://www.shopify.com/partners/blog/shopify-webhooks-how-to-prep-your-app-this-black-friday-cyber-monday) , and extension points. You can[integrate Shopify](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/apps) with warehouses, ERPs, and other systems;[customize POS workflows](https://www.shopify.com/blog/pos-customization-use-cases) with extensions; and control access by store, franchise, or user.


On the[subscriptions side](https://www.shopify.com/enterprise/blog/composable-subscriptions-shopify) , the same composable approach exposes billing APIs, webhooks, and extension points you can mix, match, and replace without rebuilding from scratch.


That means you can keep Shopify as the commerce core while connecting specialist tools around it, instead of rebuilding the whole operation when a workflow changes.


Take[The Good Guys](https://www.thegoodguys.com.au/) , for example. Their old ecommerce system was “a spiderweb of extensions and data duplications,” according to Alberto Simongini, their general manager of engineering.


After moving to Shopify, The Good Guys began using Shopify as the transactional core while layering in[Contentful](https://apps.shopify.com/contentful-sync?st_source=autocomplete&surface_detail=autocomplete_apps) for content management system (CMS),[Algolia](https://apps.shopify.com/algolia-search?st_source=autocomplete&surface_detail=autocomplete_apps) for search, and[Riskified](https://apps.shopify.com/riskified) for fraud protection through APIs. One of the biggest changes was moving from batch to event-driven data flows, so price, promotion, and product details could stay aligned in real time.


As a result, the brand reported close to 20% growth in online sales, two times faster site speed,[five times faster deployment cycles](https://www.shopify.com/case-studies/the-good-guys) , and a 50% reduction in campaign setup time.


“Shopify gave The Good Guys a strong technical foundation, and its open architecture meant we could integrate the right tools for their specific needs rather than compromise on a monolithic platform,” says Cal Wilson, founder and CEO.


### Scalability and uptime


Lastly, consider whether the platform is able to scale across locations and markets and stay performant under load.


Shopify powers millions of merchants across more than 175 countries and has processed over[$1.7 trillion in commerce](https://www.shopify.com/enterprise/blog/agentic-ready-product-data#:~:text=We%27ve%20processed%20more%20than%20%241.7%20trillion%20in%20global%20commerce%20since%20our%20inception) since inception, and it scales across stores, franchises, and users with open APIs and role-based permissions.


Shopify Plus also holds[99.99% uptime on average](https://www.shopify.com/plus#:~:text=99.99%25%20uptime,of%20the%20year) during the biggest flash sales and events of the year, backed by over 4,500 engineers building the infrastructure.


When using their old custom ecommerce platform,[Staples Canada](https://www.staples.ca/) often struggled when shopping volume peaked, and major promotions could only be deployed at night when the site came down to update.


After moving to Shopify, Staples was able to do four times more online sales promotions per day,[set all-time sales records during Black Friday Cyber Monday](https://www.shopify.com/case-studies/staples) , and handle “Black Friday–like” sales levels for 30 straight days during COVID-19 without performance issues.


“Uptime on the site has been at virtually 100%, with no degradation of performance at a time when our customers need it most,” says Andy Lee, senior director of digital product management.


## How to find the right retail operations software for you


The goal is to match your real bottlenecks to the features that resolve them.


### 1. Where does your operation break?


Use a worksheet like the one below to identify areas for improvement. Each of the problems in the lefthand column is a real-life issue one of the retailers mentioned earlier ran into.


What’s the problem? What does it cost you? What business area should you focus on?


Online and in-store stock counts disagree *\[Calculate missed sales, phantom inventory, and bloated buffer stock costs\]* Unified inventory visibility


Register goes dark when Wi-Fi drops *\[Calculate lost peak-hour revenue and walkouts\]* Offline selling and store continuity


No one can explain why a metric moved *\[Calculate engineering and analyst hours spent digging and delayed business decisions\]* Reporting and analytics


New tools won’t connect to your ERP or WMS *\[Calculate vendor lock-in fees and maintenance overhead\]* Open architecture and integrations


Site or POS buckles on peak days *\[Calculate direct holiday revenue lost and cart abandonment\]* Scalability and uptime


### 2. What’s your focus?


If you’re having issues with checkout, payments, or returns at the register, you might need stronger POS software. If the problem is store counts or replenishment, you might need[inventory management](https://www.shopify.com/blog/inventory-management) software.


If the problem is that all of your systems hold different versions of inventory, orders, products, customers, pricing, or returns, you’re likely looking for[retail operations](https://www.shopify.com/blog/retail-operations) software. A unified commerce platform like Shopify that can connect those workflows.


[Simon Pearce](https://simonpearce.com/) , a Vermont glassware brand, turned to Shopify when they realized their business was running on disconnected ecommerce, POS, and business-to-business (B2B) systems, all tied to an outdated ERP.


Their inventory updated only once a day, the POS dropped out during peak Q4 selling, and their signature custom-engraving service ran on paper forms and back-and-forth email. After consolidating with Shopify, they[collapsed three separate systems into one](https://www.shopify.com/case-studies/simon-pearce) , moved inventory from once-daily updates to real time, and ended the POS outages that had been disrupting stores.


“With our web and POS unified through Shopify, we feel good about how our technology can help us to achieve our goals as a brand,” says Lindsey Warren-Shriner, director of strategic initiatives.


### 3. What will it cost to run?


In addition to the subscription fee, you’ll need to consider hardware, payment processing, implementation, training, integration work, ongoing maintenance, downtime, and the cost of every manual workaround still in place.


When London-based bakery[Konditor](https://konditor.co.uk/) moved to Shopify, they were able to[cut costs 13% against their previous POS](https://www.shopify.com/case-studies/konditor) and ecommerce provider and spend 50% less time on admin like inventory updates.


“We avoided having to spend something like £20,000 a year just to keep our old site up to date from a security perspective, without adding any benefits to the business or customer experience,” says Tom Rundell, the company’s online operations manager.


### 4. Will it hold up in your stores?


Pick one or two stores and test the things that break. Then, train the staff who’ll use it daily, measure the time it saves against the friction it adds, then roll it out in phases.


[Nutrition Warehouse](https://www.nutritionwarehouse.com.au/) , Australia’s largest sports supplement retailer, put more than 120 stores on Shopify POS in six months and[cut staff training from a full day to 15 minutes](https://www.shopify.com/case-studies/nutrition-warehouse) .


“Our team can launch updates from HQ, automate key workflows, and empower staff to deliver a seamless customer experience—without all the manual overhead,” says COO Duncan McHugh.

## Retail operations software FAQ


### What software is used in retail?


Retailers use different types of retail software to run a retail business, including POS systems for in-store sales, inventory systems for inventory tracking, customer relationship management (CRM) tools for customer management, workforce tools for staffing, and analytics tools for measuring sales performance.


Growing retailers often need a unified platform that connects online and physical stores, orders, products, and customer data.


### Is RMS an ERP system?


A retail management system, or RMS, is not always an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system. An RMS usually helps retailers manage retail operations like inventory, sales, customers, and in-store operations. An ERP manages broader business functions such as finance, procurement, supply chain, and accounting. Some ERP systems include retail modules, but many retailers use separate retail operations tools alongside their ERP.


### Which retail software is best?


The best retail management software depends on what you need to fix. If your biggest challenge is checkout, POS may be most useful.


If stock accuracy is the issue, prioritize inventory tracking. If teams are juggling disconnected systems across online and physical stores, a retail operations platform or unified commerce platform like Shopify can help streamline operations by connecting orders, inventory, payments, and customer relationships in one place.


### What is POS software for retail?


POS software helps retailers process sales at the point of purchase. In stores, that usually means checkout, payments, receipts, returns, staff permissions, and product lookup. Modern POS systems can also connect in-store sales with ecommerce, inventory, orders, and customer data.
